title: Chapter 49 — The Hyena
paragraphs: There are certain queer times and occasions in this strange, mixed affair we call life when a man takes this whole universe for a vast practical joke, though he only dimly sees the wit of it, and more than suspects that the joke is at nobody's expense but his own. Still, nothing gets him down, and nothing seems worth arguing about. He bolts down all events, all creeds and beliefs and persuasions, all hard things visible and invisible, no matter how knobby, as an ostrich with a powerful digestion gobbles down bullets and gun flints. And as for small difficulties and worries, prospects of sudden disaster, danger to life and limb — all these, and death itself, seem to him only sly, good-natured hits and jolly punches in the ribs from the unseen and unaccountable old joker. That odd, wayward sort of mood I am speaking of comes over a man only in some time of extreme trouble; it comes in the very midst of his earnestness, so that what a moment before might have seemed to him a thing of the greatest importance now seems only part of the general joke. There is nothing like the perils of whaling to breed this free-and-easy sort of genial, desperado philosophy; and it was with this that I now regarded the whole voyage of the Pequod, and the great White Whale that was its object.

"Queequeg," I said, when they had dragged me — the last man — to the deck, and I was still shaking myself in my jacket to fling off the water, "Queequeg, my fine friend, does this sort of thing happen often?" Without much emotion, though soaked through just like me, he gave me to understand that such things did often happen.

"Mr. Stubb," I said, turning to that worthy, who, buttoned up in his oil jacket, was now calmly smoking his pipe in the rain, "Mr. Stubb, I think I have heard you say that of all whalemen you ever met, our chief mate, Mr. Starbuck, is by far the most careful and prudent. I suppose, then, that going headlong at a running whale with your sail set in a foggy squall is the height of a whaleman's discretion?"
"Certainly. I've lowered for whales from a leaking ship in a gale off Cape Horn."

"Mr. Flask," I said, turning to little King-Post, who was standing close by, "you are experienced in these things, and I am not. Will you tell me whether it is an unbreakable law in this fishery, Mr. Flask, for an oarsman to break his own back pulling himself backward into death's jaws?"

"Can't you put it more simply?" said Flask. "Yes, that's the law. I'd like to see a boat's crew backing water up to a whale face-first. Ha, ha! The whale would give them squint for squint, mind that!"

Here, then, from three impartial witnesses, I had a deliberate statement of the whole case. Considering, therefore, that squalls, capsizings in the water, and the bivouacs on the deep that follow were matters of common occurrence in this kind of life; considering that at the supremely critical instant of going on to the whale I must hand my life over to the man who steered the boat — often a fellow who, at that very moment, in his impetuousness, is on the point of sinking the craft with his own frantic stamping; considering that the particular disaster to our own particular boat was chiefly to be blamed on Starbuck's driving on to his whale almost in the teeth of a squall, and considering that Starbuck, for all that, was famous for his great caution in the fishery; considering that I belonged to this uncommonly prudent Starbuck's boat; and finally, considering what a devil's chase I was caught up in, concerning the White Whale — taking all things together, I say, I thought I might as well go below and make a rough draft of my will. "Queequeg," I said, "come along; you shall be my lawyer, executor, and legatee."

It may seem odd that sailors, of all people, should be forever tinkering with their last wills and testaments, but nobody in the world enjoys that pastime more. This was the fourth time in my life at sea that I had done it. Once the ceremony was finished this time, I felt all the easier; a stone had been rolled away from my heart. What's more, every day I lived from then on would be as good as the days Lazarus lived after he was raised from the dead — a clear extra profit of however many months or weeks it might turn out to be. I had outlived myself; my death and burial were locked away in my chest. I looked around me calmly and contentedly, like a quiet ghost with a clear conscience sitting behind the bars of a snug family vault.
Now then, I thought, unconsciously rolling up my sleeves — here goes for a cool, collected dive at death and destruction, and the devil take the hindmost.
